alignment.note: Greek employs a genitive absolute (ἐξελθόντων αὐτῶν, 'when they had gone out'); the Vulgate renders this with a cum-clause plus pluperfect subjunctive (Cumque egressi essent); the Peshitta uses a temporal ܘܟܕ ('and when') with a finite perfect ܢܦܩܘ. All three express the same circumstantial-temporal sense through distinct subordinating strategies.

The Greek genitive pronoun αὐτῶν ('they') is grammatically required to supply the subject of the genitive absolute, but both Syriac and Latin encode the subject inflectionally within the finite verb (ܢܦܩܘ / egressi essent), so no separate pronoun is transmitted.

Greek marks the noun with the article (τοῦ πλοίου, 'the boat'); the Vulgate navi and the Syriac ܣܦܝܢܬܐ use the bare/emphatic noun respectively, neither language possessing a definite article of the Greek type, so the definiteness is rendered idiomatically rather than lexically.

The Greek adverb εὐθύς ('immediately') and Latin continuo are single lexemes; the Peshitta renders the same notion with the idiomatic adverbial phrase ܒܪ ܫܥܬܗ ('in the son of its hour', i.e. 'at that very moment'), a standard Syriac periphrasis for instantaneity.
αὐτόν / eum; the Peshitta encodes the object pronoun as the suffix -ܘܗܝ on the verb ܐܣܬܟܠܘܗܝ rather than as a separate token.

The Peshitta supplies an explicit subject ܐܢܫܝ ܐܬܪܐ ('the men of the region/place') for the verb 'recognised him', whereas the Greek and Latin leave the subject implicit in the third-person plural verb. This is a clarifying expansion typical of Syriac narrative style, making explicit who did the recognising.

The Clementine Vulgate places a colon at the verse end, marking the syntactic boundary before the following clause; neither the Greek nor the Syriac transmit corresponding punctuation in this edition.
